newsitem.title: UK: Strong pound reignites UK interest rate debate.
newsitem.headline: Strong pound reignites UK interest rate debate.

text.p: The strength of sterling and its impact on UK monetary policy returned to the spotlight on Tuesday amid conflicting messages from the Bank of England and the Confederation of British Industry.

Central bank chief Eddie George gave a forthright warning late on Monday of the danger of allowing the strong pound to delay a rate rise but the CBI's quarterly industrial trends survey today indicated sterling's performance was subduing cost pressures in the manufacturing and export sectors .

The CBI survey appeared to bear out Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's decision last week to keep British rates on hold. He said then the decision was influenced by the deflationary effect of the strong pound.
But some currency analysts are unconvinced.

"To say that sterling will play the role of monetary brake is structurally false and dangerous. And if it were to be enough it would affect the wrong part of the economy anyway," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International in London.

Analysts argue the strong pound has so far had a real impact only on the export sector, which has played a relatively small role in Britain's recent economic growth. The much-vaunted consumer-led recovery, which threatens to boost inflation, is seen as being largely untouched by the currency's strength and weakness.

Sterling has risen over forty pfennigs against the mark since August 1995, touching a fresh 52-month high against the mark just above 2.70. Against the dollar, it has appreciated over 14 cents in the same period, peaking above $1.70 early this month.

Some currency analysts' sympathies were with the BOE's George, who on Monday called for a "modest pre-emptive" increase in interest rates to prevent a resurgence of inflation, particularly on the domestic front amid a tightening labour market, rising house prices and a growing services sector.

"Things are motoring ahead on that front and there are very good grounds for George to put rates up," said IBJ's Francis. "We're still in the situation where small changes in the rates can be put on without major effects."
Higher British rates have long been discounted in the currency markets and a small increase in the near term is unlikely to have a big currency impact.

A quarter point rise now, say analysts, could slow sterling down by defusing some of the speculation about higher rates being built into exchange rates, and would reinforce the government's credibility.
But the beleagured Conservative government must call a general election by late May, and has little time to tighten monetary policy.
Chancellor Clarke's rate hike in October caught many by surprise but sent the right message to the market, and possibly the electorate, analysts said.
Another rise so close to the election would probably be asking the public for too much, hence the opportune anti-inflationary argument of sterling's strength, analysts said.

"I think that it's still a situation where he (Clarke) is using what's available to justify his position which is probably more politically based," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standared Chartered Bank in London.
Analysts also said that interest rates are currently playing less of a factor in the pound's strength.

Even if rates remain unchanged, the interest rate differential between Britain and the Continent is favourable for the pound. Continued British economic growth also remains a pull for investors especially against the backdrop of fiscal belt tightening in Europe.
